Lessons.Title: Ways to Compare Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 original Grade4 Unit2 Lesson12: compare numerical fractions by conceptual size of same-part fractions and by benchmarks1/2 and1. The original four-page student task and 25-cell matrix read from teacher/source. Keep original introduction, goal, academic mapping.

Warm-up Estimation Exploration (10min): use teacher-displayed original number line point just left of one-half. Student provides too-low/about-right/too-high estimates and explains with benchmarks; teacher reviews original graphic without pretending exact location known.

Activity1 The Greatest of Them All (15min): original 25 fractions form5 rows with numerators2,4,7,11,26 and5 columns A3,B5,C10,D12,E100. Each column greatest is26 over that denominator; each row greatest is numerator/3. Whole matrix greatest26/3. Ask learner to explain the two same-numerator/denominator patterns, not just check numerical answers.

Activity2 Relative to1/2 and1 (20min): reuse the SAME 25-cell grid; classify each fraction into less-than1/2, between1/2 and1, or greater-than1. Use three different colors OR circle/triangle/square with a written legend. Student explains two rules and peer exchanges evidence.

Activity2 original four comparisons:2/5 vs7/10→7/10;4/10 vs7/12→7/12;11/100 vs4/3→4/3;26/10 vs11/12→26/10. Explain fractions relative to half and1. This prepares a later lesson's equivalence-based comparisons but does not require that as the only strategy.
Lesson synthesis10min: recognize which fraction is bigger by common numerators, denominators or half/whole benchmark. Classroom diagrams, color code, partner arguments are teacher-reviewed.

Edulytics independently authored five-minute Cool-down, NOT original publisher protected item: choose larger between2/5 and7/10, and justify why26/3 wins the original 5×5 grid. Teacher checks reasoning; existing exact numeric Practice is supplementary only.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same numerator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal number of fraction units across shares of same whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Smaller positive denominator yields larger unit part.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: Same-size fraction unit in a shared whole.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Bigger numerator means bigger fractional total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Benchmark1/2 or1
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare quantity to familiar half or whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Biggest of source grid
WorkedExamples.Question: Which of25 original fractions is greatest?
WorkedExamples.Method: Inspect each row and column pattern.
Steps: Within row, column A denominator3 gives biggest fraction.
Within column, row5 numerator26 gives biggest fraction.
WorkedExamples.Check: It exceeds8 while other25 fractions in grid are less.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent exact fraction reasoning
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is greater, 7/8 or 3/4?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert to equivalent equal-sized fractional parts and check the comparison.
Steps: Compare seven eighths with six eighths.
WorkedExamples.Check: First-party mathematical calculation; original pupil diagrams and open reasoning require separate teacher review.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Bigger written denominator must mean greater fraction.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It makes equal parts smaller when numerator fixed.
Original task requires visible code/shape key and written explanations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show legend and mathematical classification of25 source fractions.

SummaryPoints: Source original 4-page PDF; warm-up marked point slightly left of1/2 and written estimates.
Exactly25 original fractions with five numerator rows and five denominator columns; greatest26/3.
Classify all25 against1/2 and1 with teacher-reviewed shape/color key.
Four original pairs and their correct benchmark-based greater fractions.
